scope.git_search: All refs and reflogs in the published and app repositories; unique blobs at commits touching scoped paths. Published-repo unreachable blobs under 2 MB also searched.
scope.local_search: Generator backups, WIZARD_LINES declarations, explicit dialogue lists and replacement tables in the writing scripts listed in sources; current app wizard-talk.js.
scope.limits: This is all dialogue recovered from the named local sources, not a claim to recover deleted chats, garbage-collected Git objects, every prose quote, or caption-only proposals that never entered a dialogue pool. App-repo unreachable objects were not searched. Editing substrings are labelled Fragment. Git presence is not deployment proof.
scope.deduplication: Exact decoded text only. Wording, contractions, punctuation and stage directions retained. Literal source escaping is decoded; no editorial rewrite applied to archived text.

lines.text: I asked the eleven spiders in my spellbook to leave. Twelve voted against.
lines.review: The extra voter is a real improvement over unexplained spider dread. But the arithmetic and parliamentary spiders feel assembled for a neat punchline.

lines.text: I can do this twice, and then I need a rest.
lines.review: A resource limit or double entendre without a specific situation. Too generic to justify a slot.

lines.text: I can make it rain indoors. That is the point of the spell.
lines.review: Explicitly says that the odd ability has no further point. This is the dead-end sentence pattern the pool needs less of.

lines.text: I cannot heal you. Nobody ever listens to that part.
lines.review: A class distinction can give him a small working grievance. It is familiar role-playing banter and requires that audience.

lines.text: I cannot see what you share. That is rather the whole point.
lines.review: Privacy reassurance put in a fictional speaker's mouth. The character's inability to see is not a useful product guarantee.

lines.text: I cast Shared Vision
lines.review: Names a spell but does not finish an exchange. It is a title or caption starter.

lines.text: I cast Shared Vision. You are now also responsible for knowing this.
lines.review: Shared responsibility for seeing something could work between two viewers. No embarrassing shared event exists on this page to support it.

lines.text: I cast square fireballs. Corners have been getting away with things.
lines.review: Square fireballs have a visual idea; 'corners have been getting away with things' adds an unspecified grievance instead of developing it.

lines.text: I cast. I cast. I CAST. ...Give it a second.
lines.review: Repeated casting followed by a wait instruction. This imitates a comic performance without an event to sustain it.

lines.text: I could stop time right now. I will not. I want to see how this goes.
lines.review: Claims enormous power, elects not to use it, and supplies a vague reason. The reader receives no action or revealing choice.

lines.text: I could stop time right now. I will not. I want to see what you do next.
lines.review: Claims enormous power, elects not to use it, and supplies a vague reason. The reader receives no action or revealing choice.

lines.text: I could teach you. I will not.
lines.review: Refusing to teach is ordinary grumpiness. 'I have seen how that ends' hides rather than supplies the interesting part.

lines.text: I could teach you. I will not. I have seen how that ends.
lines.review: Refusing to teach is ordinary grumpiness. 'I have seen how that ends' hides rather than supplies the interesting part.

lines.text: I could turn you into a chair. I am not going to. The chair thing is behind me.
lines.review: The chair transformation is familiar; both endings evade the actual chair incident.

lines.text: I could turn you into a chair. I'm not going to. It worked once.
lines.review: The chair transformation is familiar; both endings evade the actual chair incident.

lines.text: I counted the stars twice and decided not to pursue it. The second count was different.
lines.review: A changed star count could be eerie. The line provides no reason to care, and reordering the refusal to investigate only makes it more mannered.

lines.text: I counted the stars twice. The second count was different.
lines.review: A changed star count could be eerie. The line provides no reason to care, and reordering the refusal to investigate only makes it more mannered.

lines.text: I counted the stars twice. The second count was different. I decided not to pursue it.
lines.review: A changed star count could be eerie. The line provides no reason to care, and reordering the refusal to investigate only makes it more mannered.

lines.text: I declined the throne. My newt accepted. He has flooded the ballroom.
lines.review: The newt accepting a throne is an arbitrary substitution; flooding the ballroom is the obvious animal follow-through, not a second surprise.

lines.text: I did not ask how big the room was. I cast Fireball.
lines.review: A recognisable Fireball meme repeated without a new angle.

lines.text: I did not do that. It was the orb. We are both lying.
lines.review: There is no preceding event for 'that' to denote. The confession is an author-supplied wink.

lines.text: I didn't do that. It was the orb. We're both lying.
lines.review: There is no preceding event for 'that' to denote. The confession is an author-supplied wink.

lines.text: I do not do cardio. I am a wizard.
lines.review: A generic refusal to exercise dressed in a class name.

lines.text: I do not forgive. I file.
lines.review: The filing/grudge contrast is an office slogan. No actual grudge is revealed.

lines.text: I do not hold grudges. I hold prisoners.
lines.review: A familiar threats-as-wordplay construction. More hostile than entertaining.

lines.text: I do not host your screen. I merely point at it.
lines.review: The signpost explanation is product positioning, not character dialogue. It also simplifies the transport roles too aggressively.

lines.text: I do not keep a copy. Nowhere in an orb to put one.
lines.review: A glass orb's lack of storage is used as proof of a software privacy claim. Neither sound explanation nor much of a joke.

lines.text: I do not keep a copy. There is nowhere in an orb to put one.
lines.review: A glass orb's lack of storage is used as proof of a software privacy claim. Neither sound explanation nor much of a joke.

lines.text: I do not need a Tower to show you a picture. Nobody does.
lines.review: A universal anti-server assertion delivered as fantasy defiance. The fictional terms obscure a factual claim that needs qualification.

lines.text: I do not need the orb. I like the orb.
lines.review: Simple affection for the prop is understandable. Very slight, but does not need to pretend to be a punchline.

lines.text: I do not pay my apprentice. I pay him in *knowledge*.
lines.review: An unpaid-internship joke with 'knowledge' italicised to insist on the sarcasm. Stock exploitation humour.

lines.text: I do not teleport. I arrive. There is a difference and it is mostly paperwork.
lines.review: Makes an empty distinction and then uses paperwork to fill it. A clear example of polished wording with no substance.

lines.text: I don't keep a copy. Nowhere in an orb to put one.
lines.review: A glass orb's lack of storage is used as proof of a software privacy claim. Neither sound explanation nor much of a joke.

lines.text: I dumped Constitution. Ask me how that is going.
lines.review: A character-sheet choice with a request for the reader to supply the consequence.

lines.text: I enchanted the king's soup. The croutons will know when.
lines.review: The croutons are whimsical, but what they will do is withheld. This is a setup abandoned at its most important point.

lines.text: I felt that. I have *feelings*, you know.
lines.review: A direct complaint after a poke. Plain interaction feedback, although the italicised appeal is rather needy.

lines.text: I gave the throne legs. It has chosen a different king.
lines.review: A throne choosing its king is legible wordplay with a visual consequence. Still only a short enchanted-object premise.

lines.text: I had an apprentice once. He unionised, and then he negotiated.
lines.review: Unionising is treated as inherently funny. Adding negotiation merely describes what unions do.

lines.text: I had an apprentice once. He unionised, then he negotiated.
lines.review: Unionising is treated as inherently funny. Adding negotiation merely describes what unions do.

lines.text: I had an apprentice once. He unionised.
lines.review: Unionising is treated as inherently funny. Adding negotiation merely describes what unions do.

lines.text: I have Darkvision and I am telling everyone.
lines.review: Announces a game ability and enthusiasm for it. Nothing beyond that declaration.

lines.text: I have a Wish spare. I am not spending it on rent.
lines.review: A magical windfall withheld from rent is not an interesting choice without a reason or alternative.

lines.text: I have a Wish spare. I am not wasting it on rent.
lines.review: A magical windfall withheld from rent is not an interesting choice without a reason or alternative.

lines.text: I have a component pouch and I am not afraid to use it.
lines.review: The standard 'not afraid to use it' threat with a fantasy accessory substituted.

lines.text: I have a familiar who is a cat. He is not a cat.
lines.review: Contradicts the cat premise immediately and stops. Mystery by itself is not a joke.

lines.text: I have a scroll of Wish somewhere. I am saving it for something petty.
lines.review: Promises a petty use of great magic while withholding the petty use we actually want to hear.

lines.text: I have a spell for everything. I do not remember this one.
lines.review: The forgetful expert is familiar, and 'this one' has no specific referent.

lines.text: I have a spell for making people leave. You are about to see it.
lines.review: Promises a future spell or consequence that the interaction never delivers.

lines.text: I have already cast it. You will notice in a minute.
lines.review: Promises a future spell or consequence that the interaction never delivers.

lines.text: I have an apprentice. He is on fire. That is not related to the lesson.
lines.review: An apprentice on fire is stock slapstick; denying its relevance is an extra wink, not a better incident.

lines.text: I have been asked to leave a library. I was not doing anything. They just knew.
lines.review: An unspecified reputation stands in for an incident. 'They just knew' asks the reader to invent the joke.

lines.text: I have been asked to leave three libraries. I read the books in the wrong order.
lines.review: Being banned for reading books out of order makes no sense beyond the asserted absurdity. 'Wrong' versus 'out of' does not fix it.

lines.text: I have been asked to leave three libraries. I read the books out of order.
lines.review: Being banned for reading books out of order makes no sense beyond the asserted absurdity. 'Wrong' versus 'out of' does not fix it.

lines.text: I have been asked to stop ending every meeting with a Fireball. I have declined.
lines.review: Being asked to stop using Fireball is only the setup. Refusing is the obvious response and the shortened versions remove more substance.

lines.text: I have been asked to stop ending meetings with a Fireball.
lines.review: Being asked to stop using Fireball is only the setup. Refusing is the obvious response and the shortened versions remove more substance.

lines.text: I have been audited twice. Both times I was, technically, on fire.
lines.review: An audit and being on fire are juxtaposed without a meaningful connection. 'Technically' feigns precision.

lines.text: I have been banned from nicer dimensions than this one.
lines.review: An old 'thrown out of better places' joke, or an admission of deserved bans. Both omit the behaviour that could distinguish him.

lines.text: I have been banned from three kingdoms. All three were correct to ban me.
lines.review: An old 'thrown out of better places' joke, or an admission of deserved bans. Both omit the behaviour that could distinguish him.

lines.text: I have been dead twice. The paperwork was worse.
lines.review: Death followed by worse paperwork is one of the most familiar fantasy-bureaucracy jokes.

lines.text: I have been offered a throne twice. Both times I sent the newt.
lines.review: Sending a newt instead of accepting a throne is random substitution. No reason or consequential response is supplied.

lines.text: I have been pondering my orb for nine hours. It is mostly bad news and a man selling a sword.
lines.review: A social-media feed complaint with orb and sword substituted. The nine hours are decoration, and the four versions do not discover a new observation.

lines.text: I have been scrying for six hundred years. The main thing I have learned is that people are in the bath.
lines.review: Centuries of magical experience reduced to seeing bathers is a predictable peeping joke, poorly matched to a screen-sharing site's privacy concerns.

lines.text: I have counted the stars twice. The second count was different and I have decided not to pursue it.
lines.review: A changed star count could be eerie. The line provides no reason to care, and reordering the refusal to investigate only makes it more mannered.

lines.text: I have cursed a man for a remark he made in 1408.
lines.review: An old grudge is asserted, but neither the remark nor the curse is given. The date masquerades as specificity.

lines.text: I have cursed a rival's house to be uphill from itself.
lines.review: The impossible hill is an imaginable nuisance rather than a vague threat. It still reads as a clever standalone curse rather than natural conversation.

lines.text: I have cursed every chair in this room to know what you did.
lines.review: Chairs knowing an unspecified offence has no consequence. It combines two already overused omissions.

lines.text: I have four hit points and a very good hat.
lines.review: Fragility contrasted with a good hat is a slight character-sheet caption. It does not improve with a different hit-point count elsewhere.

lines.text: I have memorised the entire sky. I did it wrong, but I have memorised it.
lines.review: Memorising the sky incorrectly sounds odd but yields no incident, explanation, or useful self-revelation.

lines.text: I have never once rolled well on a save against anything pleasant.
lines.review: The saving-throw metaphor fights the meaning: resisting something pleasant would usually be undesirable. The reader has to repair the sentence.

lines.text: I have outlived everyone who called this hat a phase.
lines.review: Outliving a fashion criticism is understandable vanity. A mild hat response, though it has the finish of a reusable quote.

lines.text: I have outlived four Councils, two kings and a goose.
lines.review: The goose is a random small item after grand institutions. Removing 'persistent' strips out the little narrative suggestion the earlier version had.

lines.text: I have outlived four Councils, two kings and a very persistent goose.
lines.review: The persistent goose at least suggests a long-running nuisance. Still a familiar grand-list-then-animal structure, too slight to call a strong joke.

lines.text: I have pierced the veil between worlds.
lines.review: A fantasy accomplishment or opening clause, retained as historical material. It supplies no exchange or payoff on its own.

lines.text: I have plenty of wards against that, you know.
lines.review: Claims magical protection but neither uses it nor says anything interesting about it.

lines.text: I have prepared the wrong spell for this.
lines.review: An ordinary mistake response if a particular attempted spell has failed. In random rotation, 'this' has no referent.

lines.text: I have read the terms of service. There are none.
lines.review: A sweeping terms-of-service assertion is a factual/legal matter disguised as a joke. The punchline is simply absence.

lines.text: I have seen the face of god. He was fine. Bit of a nerd.
lines.review: The sublime reduced to 'a nerd' is predictable bathos. 'He was fine' adds the pool's stock shrug.

lines.text: I have studied the arcane for six hundred years and I still cannot open this jar.
lines.review: All-powerful person defeated by a jar is a very familiar contrast, with six hundred years added for emphasis.

lines.text: I have taken a new apprentice. He is not on fire yet. We are both hopeful.
lines.review: An apprentice not yet on fire repeats the same tired danger gag. Announcing mutual hope is extra explanation.

lines.text: I have three hundred spells and I use four.
lines.review: Having many spells and using few is an ordinary tools-in-a-drawer observation. 'For company' tries to add sentiment without developing it.

lines.text: I have three hundred spells and I use four. The rest are for company.
lines.review: Having many spells and using few is an ordinary tools-in-a-drawer observation. 'For company' tries to add sentiment without developing it.

lines.text: I have three hundred spells. I like four of them.
lines.review: Having many spells and using few is an ordinary tools-in-a-drawer observation. 'For company' tries to add sentiment without developing it.

lines.text: I have three memories of my mother and two of them are the same memory.
lines.review: A concrete and affecting observation about memory loss. It has meaning, but this casual mascot interaction does not earn that emotional weight.

lines.text: I have three memories of my mother. Two are the same memory.
lines.review: A concrete and affecting observation about memory loss. It has meaning, but this casual mascot interaction does not earn that emotional weight.

lines.text: I insured the tower. They asked what I do. I said heat.
lines.review: Evasive insurance disclosure is a stock joke. 'Heat' is a weak euphemism doing all the work.

lines.text: I keep a comet in the cellar. It is not for anything. I just like it.
lines.review: Keeping a comet just because he likes it is comprehensible character texture. The insistence that it is not for anything over-explains a modest whim.

lines.text: I keep a comet in the cellar. It's not for anything. I just like it.
lines.review: Keeping a comet just because he likes it is comprehensible character texture. The insistence that it is not for anything over-explains a modest whim.

lines.text: I keep a list of things that have tried to eat me. It is alphabetical.
lines.review: An alphabetical or long list is ordinary. The objects on the list are withheld, leaving filing as the whole joke.

lines.text: I keep a list of things that have tried to eat me. It is alphabetical. It is long.
lines.review: An alphabetical or long list is ordinary. The objects on the list are withheld, leaving filing as the whole joke.

lines.text: I keep a list of things that have tried to eat me. It is long.
lines.review: An alphabetical or long list is ordinary. The objects on the list are withheld, leaving filing as the whole joke.

lines.text: I keep a list of things that have tried to eat me. It's alphabetical.
lines.review: An alphabetical or long list is ordinary. The objects on the list are withheld, leaving filing as the whole joke.

lines.text: I keep a mimic as a footstool. We both think we're being patient.
lines.review: A mimic waiting to eat him while he enjoys a footstool suggests a mutual standoff. The creature's motive is clearer than his, so 'both' makes the reader repair it.

lines.text: I keep the door locked. Not against anything. It is the only thing I still control.
lines.review: Loss of control is real emotional content, but this is bleak exposition rather than an earned click response.

lines.text: I levitate the cheese. The mice have built a trebuchet.
lines.review: The siege-engine image is clear and more developed than most object gags. It is also familiar cartoon escalation; prior praise overstated its originality.

lines.text: I like you. That is a warning, not a compliment.
lines.review: A generic affection-as-threat reversal. Neither the liking nor the danger has any substance.

lines.text: I lit his candle. He wants me to pay for his eyebrows.
lines.review: The original is stock singed-eyebrows slapstick. The payment rewrite is clearer but still sounds engineered to rescue an uninteresting joke.

lines.text: I lit one candle for a man. He is fine. His eyebrows are not.
lines.review: The original is stock singed-eyebrows slapstick. The payment rewrite is clearer but still sounds engineered to rescue an uninteresting joke.

lines.text: I lost my spellbook once. I do not wish to discuss it. I have prepared the same seven spells ever since, out of *spite*.
lines.review: Losing a spellbook explains repeating known spells; calling it spite does not establish whom the spite affects. The longer refusal to discuss it adds padding.

lines.text: I lost my spellbook once. I have prepared the same seven spells ever since, out of *spite*.
lines.review: Losing a spellbook explains repeating known spells; calling it spite does not establish whom the spite affects. The longer refusal to discuss it adds padding.

lines.text: I lost my spellbook once. Same seven spells ever since, out of *spite*.
lines.review: Losing a spellbook explains repeating known spells; calling it spite does not establish whom the spite affects. The longer refusal to discuss it adds padding.

lines.text: I may be slightly on fire. It is fine. It is largely decorative.
lines.review: Being on fire but calling it decorative is a stock denial of disaster. 'Slightly', 'fine', and 'largely' overwork the understatement.

lines.text: I mispronounce forbidden names until somebody corrects me.
lines.review: There is a recognisable human habit here: people cannot resist correcting a mistake. Using that to make someone else say a forbidden name gives the spell a particular purpose. Worth auditioning, not an approved keeper.

lines.text: I no longer use a mirror. The arrangement is fine. It has always been fine.
lines.review: The mirror's problem is never stated. Repeating that the arrangement is fine supplies the pose of unease without its cause.

lines.text: I no longer use a mirror. The arrangement is fine. The arrangement has always been fine.
lines.review: The mirror's problem is never stated. Repeating that the arrangement is fine supplies the pose of unease without its cause.

lines.text: I once held a gate against an army. Your screen is fine.
lines.review: Military prowess is used to reassure about a screen without any relevant connection. The boast does not establish product reliability.

lines.text: I once turned a man into a newt. He got better. He is a very good newt now, and a *passable* man.
lines.review: The familiar 'got better' newt reference is extended by literalising 'better'. The extra wording makes the borrowed joke more laboured.

lines.text: I once turned a man into a newt. He got better. He is a very good newt now.
lines.review: The familiar 'got better' newt reference is extended by literalising 'better'. The extra wording makes the borrowed joke more laboured.

lines.text: I once turned a man into a newt. He is a very good newt now.
lines.review: A good newt is a mild adjective substitution. 'He knows what he did' then withholds the only possible story.

lines.text: I once turned a man into a newt. He is a very good newt now. He knows what he did.
lines.review: A good newt is a mild adjective substitution. 'He knows what he did' then withholds the only possible story.

lines.text: I only know one spell and I have made it everyone's problem.
lines.review: A recognisable 'made it everyone's problem' caption. Nothing specifies how this wizard actually does that.

lines.text: I open presents with Mage Hand. My friends say it spoils the surprise.
lines.review: Suspicious presents could make remote opening funny, but the reader has to infer trapped gifts for 'spoils the surprise' to mean much.

lines.text: I opened a window between realms
lines.review: A fantasy accomplishment or opening clause, retained as historical material. It supplies no exchange or payoff on its own.

lines.text: I owe the demon a favour. He has not decided what.
lines.review: A future demonic favour is a story hook, not a finished remark. Withholding the favour is the entire ending.

lines.text: I predate several laws of nature. I am exempt.
lines.review: An ancient-being exemption is a polished boast. It names no law or consequence that would make the claim interesting.

lines.text: I prepare my spells each morning. Today: seven ways to leave a room.
lines.review: Over-preparing to leave a room conveys reluctance to socialise. Modest character material, though the seven methods remain unspecified.

lines.text: I prepare my spells each morning. Today: seven ways to leave a room. I am not leaving.
lines.review: The added refusal to leave undercuts the earlier idea without giving a reason. More words have made the character's intention less legible.

lines.text: I prepare my spells each morning. Today: seven ways to leave a room. I'm not leaving.
lines.review: The added refusal to leave undercuts the earlier idea without giving a reason. More words have made the character's intention less legible.

lines.text: I prepare my spells every morning. Today I prepared seven different ways to leave a room.
lines.review: Over-preparing to leave a room conveys reluctance to socialise. Modest character material, though the seven methods remain unspecified.

lines.text: I put a curse on my own left hand. It knows why.
lines.review: The hand is blamed for something unspecified. 'It knows why' has repeatedly been mistaken for a payoff in this pool.

lines.text: I put a second moon up for my own use. Stop looking at it.
lines.review: Private ownership of a visible moon has potential, but the impossible instruction to stop looking is the whole joke as written.

lines.text: I put a silence spell on my bedroom. The nightmares have to mime.
lines.review: Silent nightmares miming is an immediate visual image. It is mild rather than empty; previous reviews were too categorical in dismissing every simple premise.

lines.text: I put a truth spell on the kettle. It has stopped whistling and started naming names.
lines.review: The kettle's revelations are exactly what is withheld. 'Naming names' is a stock promise of scandal.

lines.text: I read the books in the wrong order.
lines.review: A replacement substring recovered from an editing script, not evidence of a separately spoken full line. Review it with its library or Tower sentence.

lines.text: I read the books out of order.
lines.review: A replacement substring recovered from an editing script, not evidence of a separately spoken full line. Review it with its library or Tower sentence.

lines.text: I said behold. Not backseat.
lines.review: A compact complaint about an audience interfering could work in a shared-viewing exchange. There is no such interference in this bubble interaction.

lines.text: I saw your whole future once. It was fine. You are fine. Do not worry about it.
lines.review: Repeated reassurance conventionally implies trouble but supplies none. Vague anxiety is doing the work of a joke.

lines.text: I saw your whole future once. It was fine. You're fine. Don't worry about it.
lines.review: Repeated reassurance conventionally implies trouble but supplies none. Vague anxiety is doing the work of a joke.

lines.text: I scry at sixty frames a second.
lines.review: A frame-rate claim and a bargaining orb mix product numbers with arbitrary personification. 'We compromised' never even says what the compromise was.

lines.text: I scry at sixty frames a second. The orb wanted thirty.
lines.review: A frame-rate claim and a bargaining orb mix product numbers with arbitrary personification. 'We compromised' never even says what the compromise was.

lines.text: I scry at sixty frames a second. The orb wanted thirty. We compromised.
lines.review: A frame-rate claim and a bargaining orb mix product numbers with arbitrary personification. 'We compromised' never even says what the compromise was.

lines.text: I scry the weather. I do not change it. I just like being right.
lines.review: Using foresight for the pleasure of being right is a coherent small vanity. Mild, but more believable than the grand random threats.

lines.text: I see you've opened a menu. So have I. Mine has species.
lines.review: A species menu relates to right-clicking, but the parallel 'So have I. Mine has...' is conspicuously written. It is a transformation threat in a new wrapper.

lines.text: I solved the wasp nest. The wasps are solved. The shed is also solved.
lines.review: Repeating 'solved' obscures a predictable destroyed-shed outcome. The euphemism is worked harder than the incident merits.

lines.text: I summoned a demon to hold my ladder. It offered me a kingdom. I pointed at the ladder.
lines.review: Rejecting a kingdom because he still needs the ladder held reveals a particular practical priority. It has an actual exchange and a concrete ending; still needs the owner's taste check.

lines.text: I talk to the fire. The fire talks back, but it is polite about it.
lines.review: A polite talking fire is merely a whimsical assertion. Nothing in the exchange is supplied.

lines.text: I taught a rock to count. It has got to nine. It is very pleased.
lines.review: The pleased counting rock is a small affectionate image. It can be texture, but prior reviews should not have elevated it into a strong joke.

lines.text: I taught my front door to recognise threats. It has locked me out.
lines.review: The draft repairs the door's logic but lands on a very familiar backfiring-instructions joke. Correctness is not enough reason to retain it.

lines.text: I taught my front door to recognise threats. It now opens before I reach it.
lines.review: A threat-recognising door opening for him does not establish whether it welcomes or fears him. The supposed punchline depends on filling that gap.

lines.text: I taught the fire to read. It only reads poetry now.
lines.review: Poetry is an arbitrary preference assigned to fire. Without a consequence it is merely decorative sentience.

lines.text: I told a man his future. He said it was not worth the money. He was right, which was worse.
lines.review: A dissatisfied fortune-telling customer could be promising, but the wording muddles what he was right about and then explains that it was worse.

lines.text: I turned the local HOA into a single, very confused goose.
lines.review: Turning a homeowners' association into a goose pairs two comic targets without a meaningful connection. 'Very confused' is ornamental.

lines.text: I turned the moon slightly purple. It is fine. It is a look.
lines.review: An unusual moon colour is excused as a look. This is a generic social-media shrug with a larger object.

lines.text: I use Mage Hand to turn my rival's pages before he's finished.
lines.review: Turning a page too early is a specific, recognisable irritation. The magic enables the petty act rather than replacing the joke with an arbitrary noun.

lines.text: I use divination to win arguments I had last week.
lines.review: Revisiting lost arguments is recognisable pettiness. The divination does not explain how he wins them afterward, so the mechanism is fuzzier than the page-turning line.

lines.text: I was a professor for two hundred years. I gave one lecture.
lines.review: One lecture over two centuries is an exaggeration without a clear meaning: extremely long lecture or extremely little work?

lines.text: I was a professor for two hundred years. I gave one lecture. They made me chair of the department.
lines.review: The department-chair ending reveals an ordinary academic-promotion gag after the ambiguous lecture premise. Fantasy age mostly pads it.

lines.text: I was asked to light one ceremonial candle. There was a ceremony. It was brief.
lines.review: The ceremonial fire mishap is only implied; repeating 'ceremony' and saying it was brief spends words dodging the actual event.

lines.text: I was going to be an illusionist. There was a waiting list. Fire had an opening.
lines.review: Career choice by waiting list is standard bureaucracy parody. 'Fire had an opening' does not develop the pun into anything particular.

lines.text: I was going to destroy the Council. I had a whole afternoon planned.
lines.review: Threatening to destroy a Council because there is time available is generic disproportion. Planning versus free time changes cadence, not the idea.

lines.text: I was going to destroy the Council. I had the afternoon free.
lines.review: Threatening to destroy a Council because there is time available is generic disproportion. Planning versus free time changes cadence, not the idea.

lines.text: I was not responsible. I was present. That was enough for the committee.
lines.review: An unfair committee is a familiar grievance. The actual charge and the wizard's involvement are absent.

lines.text: I went to the market on Tuesday. I did not come back until 1604.
lines.review: Tuesday and 1604 belong to different measures of time; juxtaposing them signals absurdity without a coherent journey or consequence.

lines.text: I will not tell you the material component. You would try it.
lines.review: Withholds the component that would have to make the joke interesting.

lines.text: I'm not allowed within four hundred yards of a haystack. Any haystack.

lines.text: My cat sleeps in the summoning circle. The demons have learned to arrive quietly.

lines.text: My cat walks through walls. He makes me open doors as a matter of principle.
lines.review: A cat demanding an unnecessary door opening is recognisable behaviour. A coherent mild joke, but hardly new enough to rescue the whole pool.

lines.text: My familiar has a familiar. I was not consulted.

lines.text: My familiar is a cat. He does not help. He is not supposed to help.

lines.text: My golem asked whether my bones were structural or decorative.
lines.review: A golem's confusion about bones fits its constructed body. It is a curious question rather than a finished joke, and should be judged as such.

lines.text: My medal for restraint was found three miles from the ceremony.
lines.review: An award for restraint found far away invites a comic inference. But we do not know whether it was thrown, blasted, or lost; earlier praise confidently invented the incident.

lines.text: My obituary was published in 1509. Nobody corrected it. I stopped bringing it up.
lines.review: The uncorrected obituary suggests loneliness and withdrawal. It is meaningful, but the site has not earned that melancholy relationship with the visitor.

lines.text: My orb is buffering. MY ORB IS BUFFERING.
lines.review: A repeated buffering complaint with capitals for volume. No observation beyond frustration.

lines.text: My passive Perception is nine. Nine.

lines.text: My reflection is a minute ahead. I make him taste the soup.
lines.review: The reflection's head start has a practical use, but a reader must invent how it tastes physical soup and reports back. A neat premise, not the unqualified keeper earlier reviews claimed.

lines.text: My rival demanded a duel at dawn. I have postponed the sun.

lines.text: My shadow has started carrying a staff. We have not discussed this.

lines.text: My sign says SCRIES, REASONABLE RATES. Nobody has ever asked about the rates.
lines.review: Nobody asking about rates is ambiguous: no customers, free service, or accepted prices? The sign's specificity does not resolve the joke.

lines.text: My spellbook has a bookmark in it. It has been on the same page since the war.

lines.text: My tower has forty rooms and I use three. The rest are for the echo.

lines.text: That was a cantrip, by the way.
lines.review: Could follow an impressive visible spell. As a random line it refers to an absent feat.

lines.text: That's a painted triangle. You can press harder, but I painted it quite thoroughly.
lines.review: The rejected draft labours the word 'painted' to excuse a non-playing icon. 'Quite thoroughly' is forced cleverness around a UI problem.

lines.text: The Council asked me not to end meetings with Fireball. I now open with it.
lines.review: Opening rather than ending a meeting with Fireball is a predictable malicious-compliance joke. A complete construction was previously mistaken for sufficient quality.

lines.text: The Council calls me unstable. It meets in a room that does not exist on Thursdays.
lines.review: Uses two meanings of unstable, then adds an arbitrary Thursday. The Council's absent room is a disconnected oddity rather than a persuasive comeback.

lines.text: The Council calls me unstable. The same Council meets in a room that does not exist on Thursdays.
lines.review: Uses two meanings of unstable, then adds an arbitrary Thursday. The Council's absent room is a disconnected oddity rather than a persuasive comeback.

lines.text: The Council has banned my entire school of magic. I am the entire school.
lines.review: The lone school member makes a ban personal but the sentence already implies that. The repetition of 'entire school' overstates a minor reveal.

lines.text: The Council has banned that. I have a permit.
lines.review: A ban answered by a permit is an unsupported bureaucratic contradiction.

lines.text: The Council has nineteen members and none of them can open a door.
lines.review: Nineteen incompetent council members is an unsupported insult. The door is another arbitrary object chosen to make incompetence sound concrete.

lines.text: The Council has outlawed my entire school of magic. I am the entire school.
lines.review: The lone school member makes a ban personal but the sentence already implies that. The repetition of 'entire school' overstates a minor reveal.

lines.text: The Council is not a government. It is a queue with a hat.
lines.review: A queue with a hat is a striking-sounding phrase with no useful relationship to a governing Council. This is precisely empty metaphor.

lines.text: The Council respects me. (The Council is wrong about most things.)
lines.review: A familiar self-deprecating respect joke. The parenthesis insists on the irony rather than giving the Council a specific mistaken belief.

lines.text: The Council revoked my title. I revoked their stairs.
lines.review: Removing stairs is an understandable petty retaliation. 'Revoked their stairs' strains the verb to obtain symmetry; earlier reviews praised that symmetry too readily.

lines.text: The Council voted to ban Fireball. I had voted twice.
lines.review: Voting twice might be cheating or enthusiasm for a ban. The line leaves the intended point unclear, and tense edits do not fix it.

lines.text: The Council voted to ban Fireball. I voted twice.
lines.review: Voting twice might be cheating or enthusiasm for a ban. The line leaves the intended point unclear, and tense edits do not fix it.

lines.text: The Council voted to ban Fireball. I'd voted twice.
lines.review: Voting twice might be cheating or enthusiasm for a ban. The line leaves the intended point unclear, and tense edits do not fix it.

lines.text: The Tower bills per head. My hydra is furious.
lines.review: Per-head billing applied to a hydra is a stock literalism. It also leans on an undefined Tower business; earlier 'modest but complete' approval was too permissive.

lines.text: The Tower charges extra to show my beard. Apparently I count as a group call.
lines.review: A beard does not imply multiple callers. The billing punchline depends on an unexplained equivalence.

lines.text: The Tower is a server and a staircase. They call it a Tower so you do not ask.
lines.review: Server-and-staircase is a label swap, followed by an unspecified secret. Neither explains the satire it asks the reader to recognise.

lines.text: The Tower is one server and a staircase. They call it a Tower so nobody asks.
lines.review: Server-and-staircase is a label swap, followed by an unspecified secret. Neither explains the satire it asks the reader to recognise.

lines.text: The abyss stared back. I asked it to move its cursor.
lines.review: A cursor obscuring a shared image is a real irritation, but the abyss quote supplies most of the wit. It fits a two-viewer caption better than this interaction.

lines.text: The beard has gone sentient again. Do not make eye contact.
lines.review: Making the beard sentient is the whole idea. The eye-contact warning is another unspecified consequence.

lines.text: The beard's gone sentient again. Don't make eye contact.
lines.review: Making the beard sentient is the whole idea. The eye-contact warning is another unspecified consequence.

lines.text: The blasted devils want to hold the middle of every conversation. I am a wizard, not a landlord.
lines.review: The middle-of-conversation/landlord metaphor is muddy and repeatedly explained. It delivers an ideological complaint rather than a joke.

lines.text: The blasted devils want to hold the middle of every conversation. I hold the middle of nothing. I am a wizard, not a landlord.
lines.review: The middle-of-conversation/landlord metaphor is muddy and repeatedly explained. It delivers an ideological complaint rather than a joke.

lines.text: The book of forbidden spells won't shut up about them.
lines.review: A book discussing forbidden material too eagerly is legible wordplay. Very slight, and another chatty object in a pool already full of them.

lines.text: The cat is the only one here who is not mad. He stays in.
lines.review: The cat's sanity and confinement are asserted without explaining their relationship. The longer 'that is why' makes the missing logic more obvious.

lines.text: The cat is the only one here who is not mad. That is why I do not let him out.
lines.review: The cat's sanity and confinement are asserted without explaining their relationship. The longer 'that is why' makes the missing logic more obvious.

lines.text: The devils of the great towers will happily rent you your own reflection. I find that rude.
lines.review: Renting a reflection is an abstract anti-platform metaphor. 'Rude' and 'Anyway' act as knowing closers without adding an incident or insight.

lines.text: The golem has started asking questions. Good ones. That is worse.
lines.review: The golem's questions could be interesting; the line chooses to hide all of them.

lines.text: The great glowing towers shall fall, as all towers do. I have seen it. It was a Tuesday.
lines.review: A grand prediction deflated by an arbitrary weekday. The Tuesday supplies tone instead of meaning.

lines.text: The green one is not a flavour. It is a warning.
lines.review: Colour being 'not a flavour' is a strained distinction. The warning version then explains what was already implied.

lines.text: The hat is where the power is. Do not touch the hat.
lines.review: States a hat-power premise and gives a generic warning. It does not reward discovering the hat interaction.

lines.text: The imp wants a reference. I am not giving him a reference.
lines.review: A refused reference raises a question about the imp but never answers it. Repeating 'reference' does not supply a reason.

lines.text: The last mage who tried that is now a tasteful arrangement of furniture.
lines.review: A furniture-transformation threat with 'tasteful' added as decoration. The original offence and the result are both vague.

lines.text: The mirror shows me someone older. I have asked him to leave.
lines.review: Treating an aged reflection as an unwanted visitor is understandable denial. A familiar ageing joke, but at least coherent.

lines.text: The necromancer licks a finger to turn the page. I wish he would use his own.
lines.review: The borrowed finger is a clear physical gag suited to a necromancer. Familiar macabre wordplay; worth recognising as modest rather than meaningless.

lines.text: The neighbour's dog barked at me once. The neighbour is a dog now. Everyone is fine.
lines.review: Punishing the neighbour for the dog's barking has no particular logic. 'Everyone is fine' is another unearned ironic reassurance.

lines.text: The newt knows what it did.
lines.review: The newt is made ominous without telling us anything interesting about it.

lines.text: The orb and I have an understanding. It shows me things. I pretend to be surprised.
lines.review: A normal act of viewing is described as a secret arrangement. Pretending surprise does not reveal anything worth concealing.

lines.text: The orb has a refresh rate and I have opinions about it.
lines.review: Says the wizard has opinions but withholds every opinion. A particularly clear empty teaser.

lines.text: The orb is a screen. I am a wizard. Keep up.
lines.review: Two definitions followed by condescension. 'Keep up' supplies attitude in place of humour.

lines.text: The orb says I have been looking at the orb too long. The orb is a hypocrite.
lines.review: A screen-time notification called hypocritical is familiar internet commentary. Swapping in the orb does not make it fresh.

lines.text: The orb shows me many things. Mostly it shows me that the orb wants dusting.
lines.review: The instrument of grand visions needs cleaning. A modest domestic observation, though the repeated 'orb shows' wording is laboured.

lines.text: The orb shows the future. It is the present, with more forms.
lines.review: The future as more paperwork is generic pessimism. No form or consequence makes it particular.

lines.text: The picture goes straight from your orb to theirs. No Tower. No toll.
lines.review: Repeats the direct-connection sales claim in fantasy terms. Absolute 'nothing in the middle' formulations also blur coordination and relay roles; these are not reliable product explanations.

lines.text: The picture is cut into squares and each square is *described* to the other machine. Nothing that arrives is a picture. It is a rumour of a picture.
lines.review: The 'rumour of a picture' metaphor becomes progressively more abstract through revision. Neither a good joke nor a sufficiently clear explanation of encoding.

lines.text: The potion is green. That is not a flavour. That is a warning.
lines.review: Colour being 'not a flavour' is a strained distinction. The warning version then explains what was already implied.

lines.text: The prophecy is view-only. Stop trying to change your fate.
lines.review: Read-only prophecy is neat software/fate wordplay, but reads as a caption and presumes an attempt to edit fate that has not occurred.

lines.text: The relay is a last resort, like asking a stranger for directions.
lines.review: A relay is compared to asking directions, which confuses carrying traffic with finding a route. The comparison has little comic reward anyway.

lines.text: The ring is cursed. Put it on. I want to hear the accent.
lines.review: A curse giving an accent is arbitrary; the actual accent and its effect are withheld.

lines.text: The screaming is normal. It is when it stops that you should worry.
lines.review: A stock horror reversal: silence is worse than screaming. No new situation earns its reuse.

lines.text: The spell is called screen sharing. I did not name it.
lines.review: Names the product activity and disclaims naming it. The disclaimer offers no interesting objection to the name.

lines.text: The tower burned down. Not my department.
lines.review: A disaster met with 'not my department' is standard bureaucracy comedy. Adding that people asked him merely repeats the deflection.

lines.text: The tower burned down. Not my department. They asked me anyway.
lines.review: A disaster met with 'not my department' is standard bureaucracy comedy. Adding that people asked him merely repeats the deflection.

lines.text: The tower has a room I do not open. The room is fine with this.
lines.review: An unopened room consenting to be unopened is personification without consequence.

lines.text: The walls have been in the wrong place since Tuesday.
lines.review: Misplaced walls are a premise; Tuesday and 'I have adjusted' add a deadpan pose without explaining how he lives with it.

lines.text: The walls have been in the wrong place since Tuesday. I have adjusted.
lines.review: Misplaced walls are a premise; Tuesday and 'I have adjusted' add a deadpan pose without explaining how he lives with it.

lines.text: The young mages say I am a bit much. I am exactly the correct amount.
lines.review: A familiar 'too much / correct amount' self-acceptance quote. It could be assigned to any sarcastic mascot.

lines.text: There are eight schools of magic. I have been asked to leave four of them.
lines.review: Plays on schools as institutions while withholding the expulsions. A familiar pun plus an empty reputation boast.

lines.text: There is a spider in my boot. I have dealt with it proportionately.
lines.review: The response to the spider is exactly the information that could be funny, and 'proportionately' hides it.

lines.text: There is no problem a Fireball cannot solve.
lines.review: The familiar claim that fire solves every problem by creating another. The several punctuation and contraction passes never add a fresh incident.

lines.text: There is no problem a Fireball cannot solve. Only problems that become *different* problems.

lines.text: There is no subscription. I accept no tribute.
lines.review: A pricing statement translated into tribute. Too slight to justify duplicating the page's pricing information through the mascot.

lines.text: There's no problem a Fireball can't solve. There are only problems that become different problems.
lines.review: The familiar claim that fire solves every problem by creating another. The several punctuation and contraction passes never add a fresh incident.

lines.text: They asked me to stop ending meetings with a Fireball.
lines.review: Being asked to stop using Fireball is only the setup. Refusing is the obvious response and the shortened versions remove more substance.

lines.text: They call it a Tower so nobody asks.
lines.review: A replacement substring recovered from an editing script, not evidence of a separately spoken full line. Review it with its library or Tower sentence.

lines.text: They call it a Tower so you do not ask.
lines.review: A replacement substring recovered from an editing script, not evidence of a separately spoken full line. Review it with its library or Tower sentence.

lines.text: They gave me a medal. The medal is in a drawer. The drawer is in the tower. The tower is a hole.
lines.review: The drawer-to-tower-to-hole chain is conspicuously constructed to delay a familiar destroyed-building reveal.

lines.text: They took the title over 'conduct'. I stand by the conduct.
lines.review: Stands by unspecified conduct after an unspecified charge. Two opportunities to reveal character are both withheld.

lines.text: They took the title. They let me keep the hat.
lines.review: Losing the title while retaining the hat is a modest material consolation. The words are clear; the joke is simply very small.

lines.text: This circle is load-bearing.
lines.review: A familiar load-bearing joke attached to a magical circle. It does not explain what the circle supports or create a useful interaction.

lines.text: This is not a prophecy. This idiot is doing it right now.
lines.review: Could caption a real scene of current folly. Here 'this idiot' has no established subject, so it becomes vague contempt.

lines.text: This is undignified and I will remember it.
lines.review: An ordinary promise to remember an indignity, with no particular way of remembering it.

lines.text: This one shares your screen across a road you already own. Nothing sits in the middle of it. That is the entire arrangement.
lines.review: Repeats the direct-connection sales claim in fantasy terms. Absolute 'nothing in the middle' formulations also blur coordination and relay roles; these are not reliable product explanations.

lines.text: Though you have been shunned by the archmages of the Towers, you shall find refuge here, my dear friend.
lines.review: Invents rejection in the visitor's past and offers grandiose refuge. It is presumptuous brand sentiment rather than dialogue.

lines.text: Three hundred years I have scried. Two hundred of them were buffering.
lines.review: Centuries spent buffering is an old waiting joke with inflated numbers. Changing age and removing verbs only tunes the same familiar idea.

lines.text: Tiny Hut. Eight hours. Nothing gets in. It is a *tent*.
lines.review: Describes a protective shelter and calls it a tent. Long spell names and emphatic italics cannot turn the description into a joke.

lines.text: Touch the rune. Nothing will happen.
lines.review: Invites an action and says it does nothing. Calling that the whole demonstration still does not make it rewarding.

lines.text: Touch the rune. That is the whole demonstration.
lines.review: Invites an action and says it does nothing. Calling that the whole demonstration still does not make it rewarding.

lines.text: Towers? Archmages? They teach the new ones *nothing* at the academy, I see.
lines.review: Grumbling that an academy teaches nothing is a generic elder complaint. 'Towers' adds terminology without substance.

lines.text: Twelve hit points and a dream.
lines.review: Stock underdog meme with a hit-point number inserted. Neither number makes it this wizard's joke.

lines.text: Twenty-foot radius. It does not check who else is standing there.
lines.review: Explains indiscriminate damage, then sometimes labels it a feature. Familiar game banter, not a fresh observation.

lines.text: Twenty-foot radius. It does not check who else is standing there. That is a feature.
lines.review: Explains indiscriminate damage, then sometimes labels it a feature. Familiar game banter, not a fresh observation.

lines.text: Two devices, one orb, nothing in the middle. Oldest spell there is.

lines.text: Two mages, two orbs, no middleman.
lines.review: Repeats the direct-connection sales claim in fantasy terms. Absolute 'nothing in the middle' formulations also blur coordination and relay roles; these are not reliable product explanations.

lines.text: Two orbs. One picture. No Tower in the middle.
lines.review: Repeats the direct-connection sales claim in fantasy terms. Absolute 'nothing in the middle' formulations also blur coordination and relay roles; these are not reliable product explanations.

lines.text: Ufh~
lines.review: A stylised grunt with a coy tilde. It adds affect without a recognisable character response.

lines.text: Urngghhh... you stepped on my seals. Again.
lines.review: Right-clicking is not stepping on seals. The invented bodily complaint does not fit the action.

lines.text: WE LOVE CASTING SCREENS.
lines.review: An adapted chanting meme. It belongs with a group image or caption, not as evidence of an original wizard voice.

lines.text: Wands sold separately.
lines.review: Packaging parody can work on merchandise. In a speech bubble this reads as a label, and a series of these quickly becomes filler.

lines.text: Wards! Do you think I stand in an open circle for *fun*?
lines.review: A rhetorical question asserts a need for wards without revealing anything about them. Mostly loud fantasy vocabulary.

lines.text: Well met, apprentice. I was pondering my orb. It ponders back, sometimes.
lines.review: A stock fantasy welcome gains an orb that ponders back. Sentience is the only extra idea; dropping 'sometimes' does not improve it.

lines.text: Well met, apprentice. I was pondering my orb. It ponders back.
lines.review: A stock fantasy welcome gains an orb that ponders back. Sentience is the only extra idea; dropping 'sometimes' does not improve it.

lines.text: What the Frick dude.
lines.review: A generic exclamation with conspicuous mild profanity. No character-specific observation.

lines.text: Whoa—! Put me down, I am *working*.
lines.review: A clear protest while being dragged. It fits the gesture, although 'working' supplies no special joke and the punctuation is broad.

lines.text: Windows sends. Android sees. No account, no me watching.
lines.review: Platform roles are chopped into fragments, then padded with privacy reassurance or an unexplained warning not to be weird. Neither good copy nor good humour.

lines.text: Windows sends. Android sees. No account, no subscription, no me watching.

lines.text: Windows sends. Android watches. Do not make it weird.

lines.text: Windows sends. Android watches. Don't make it weird.

lines.text: Wizard. Witch. Enchanter. Sibling. I have been all of these and the orb has never once complained.
lines.review: A character can have an inclusive personal history, but the list mixes unrelated categories and the orb's approval does not explain their significance. Needs actual context.

lines.text: Wizard. Witch. Enchanter. Sibling. The orb has never once complained.
lines.review: A character can have an inclusive personal history, but the list mixes unrelated categories and the orb's approval does not explain their significance. Needs actual context.

lines.text: Wizards who need both hands to cast have never had a decent sandwich.
lines.review: A sandwich interfering with spell gestures is a recognisable practical inconvenience. A mild game-world observation, not an exceptional joke.

lines.text: Xyzzy! ...Nothing happens. That is the joke. It has always been the joke.
lines.review: Explicitly declares that nothing happening is the joke. This is the clearest form of explaining away absent material.

lines.text: Xyzzy! ...Nothing. It has never worked. I will keep saying it.
lines.review: A borrowed magic-word reference followed by repeated failure. The persistence is ordinary, and centuries of it are only inflation.

lines.text: Xyzzy! ...Nothing. It's never worked. I'll keep saying it.
lines.review: A borrowed magic-word reference followed by repeated failure. The persistence is ordinary, and centuries of it are only inflation.

lines.text: Xyzzy! ...Nothing. Six hundred years and it has never once worked, and I will keep saying it.
lines.review: A borrowed magic-word reference followed by repeated failure. The persistence is ordinary, and centuries of it are only inflation.

lines.text: Yawn.
lines.review: A yawn could be a timed idle reaction. Randomly telling a visitor 'Yawn' can instead sound bored with them.

lines.text: Yes I could just teleport. I like the walk.
lines.review: A straightforward preference for walking. Simple character texture is allowed, but there is no need to market it as comedy.

lines.text: Yes I could teleport. The horse needs the exercise.
lines.review: Considering the horse gives the choice a small humane reason. Pleasant and slight, rather than a strong joke.

lines.text: Yes. Yes. I heard you the first time.
lines.review: As the first greeting, it rebukes a visitor who has only clicked once. It could serve repeated pokes, but moving it to first made the context worse.

lines.text: Yes? Most people knock on the door.
lines.review: The rejected opener makes clicking an image equivalent to knocking on a person. Mild, visibly manufactured etiquette wordplay.

lines.text: Yo hello — is this thing on? *taps orb* ...It is on. Splendid.
lines.review: A first-contact microphone-check style greeting. Too many greetings and performed pauses make it broad; it is usable only as an opener, not a joke.

lines.text: You are about to flinch. *does not move* ...There.
lines.review: Declares that the visitor flinched without observing them. The claimed successful trick is supplied entirely by the writer.

lines.text: You are about to flinch. There. I did not even move.
lines.review: Declares that the visitor flinched without observing them. The claimed successful trick is supplied entirely by the writer.

lines.text: You are clicking me. I can feel it.
lines.review: Acknowledges the actual click. Plain but accurate; sufficient for feedback, insufficient as a reason to keep a large dialogue pool.

lines.text: You are doing fine. I have seen archmages do worse with a better hat.
lines.review: Generic encouragement padded with unspecified inferior archmages and better equipment. It flatters the visitor without knowing what they did.

lines.text: You are doing fine. I have seen archmages do worse with a full spellbook and a better hat.
lines.review: Generic encouragement padded with unspecified inferior archmages and better equipment. It flatters the visitor without knowing what they did.

lines.text: You are here about the scrying. Everyone is here about the scrying.
lines.review: Presumes a reason for the visitor's click and repeats it. It neither answers the gesture nor reveals a worthwhile thought.

lines.text: You are prodding a millennium-old mage like a suspicious melon.
lines.review: The suspicious-melon comparison is conspicuously quirky. Correcting the age fixes continuity, not the forced simile.

lines.text: You are the first person to speak to me this week. It is Thursday.
lines.review: A lonely remark with real emotional content. It can make the visitor feel responsible for him; the casual page interaction has not established that relationship.

lines.text: You are the third person today. The other two are furniture.
lines.review: Two earlier visitors transformed into furniture is an obvious threat. The count serves the construction rather than a believable recollection.

lines.text: You can see every possible future and all your advice is "dodge."
lines.review: The uselessly broad advice is a clear divination joke between peers. The current visitor has offered no such advice, so the speaker lacks an addressee.

lines.text: You cannot eat the moon just because you own the tides. By the Nine, they are trying.
lines.review: Moon ownership and tides are thrown into a grand accusation with no clear subject or scenario. Fantasy vocabulary hides an incoherent complaint.

lines.text: You cannot simply *move* a wizard. There are runes. There are implications.
lines.review: Lists runes and implications while withholding the implications. Exactly the sort of ominous nothingness that should not return.

lines.text: You do not need an account to look into an orb.
lines.review: Repeats the no-account pitch through an orb metaphor. The longer version adds an obvious requirement rather than a punchline.

lines.text: You do not need an account to look into an orb. You need an orb.
lines.review: Repeats the no-account pitch through an orb metaphor. The longer version adds an obvious requirement rather than a punchline.

lines.text: You have taken me out of my circle. Let us not find out what happens.
lines.review: Promises that leaving the circle matters while refusing to say how. The extra versions only lengthen the withheld consequence.

lines.text: You have taken me out of my circle. Nobody knows what happens out of the circle. Let us not be the ones who find out.

lines.text: You have taken me out of my circle. Nobody knows what happens out of the circle. Let us not find out.

lines.text: You need a licence for that. I am the licence.
lines.review: A licence answered by 'I am the licence' is a generic authority boast without a comprehensible rule behind it.

lines.text: You pressed the little triangle. Nothing is loaded. There is nothing *to* load.
lines.review: Explains that the apparent play control does not play anything, twice. This rationalises an interface disappointment rather than producing a joke.

lines.text: You will do fine. You already know more than the people who will tell you that you cannot.

lines.text: Your picture travels as a great many small numbers. Each one is very brave.
lines.review: Calling numbers brave supplies cuteness in place of technical explanation or a joke.

lines.text: Your pixels travel directly to your friend. I am a signpost, not a toll booth.
lines.review: The signpost/toll-booth contrast is marketing rhetoric and oversimplifies connection routes. It should not carry factual assurance through a fictional character.

lines.text: Your screen, in my orb, nobody in between.
lines.review: Repeats the direct-connection sales claim in fantasy terms. Absolute 'nothing in the middle' formulations also blur coordination and relay roles; these are not reliable product explanations.

lines.text: Your screen, in my orb, nobody in between. That is the whole spell.
lines.review: Repeats the direct-connection sales claim in fantasy terms. Absolute 'nothing in the middle' formulations also blur coordination and relay roles; these are not reliable product explanations.

lines.text: bro is not pondering. bro is spectating.
lines.review: A viewing caption in an audience voice. Slang alone does not disqualify it, but it is not this wizard addressing the clicker.

lines.text: he'll be back. he has to check on the orb.
lines.review: A caption about someone else's behaviour, requiring a visible person returning to an orb. That scene is absent here.

lines.text: i know it's not mine. i'm showing you.
lines.review: A conversational correction whose accusation is missing. Potentially natural in a comic exchange, incomplete as random dialogue.

lines.text: my orb doesn't forget.
lines.review: A vague ominous memory claim with no incident. It also sits awkwardly beside claims that the orb keeps no copy.

lines.text: nothing. it's been nothing for two hours.
lines.review: An answer to an absent question about what the orb shows. Could belong to a comic about waiting; alone it is empty.

lines.text: shared vision. separate bad decisions.
lines.review: A slogan-shaped caption for two people making a mistake together. No actual decision gives it substance in the bubble.

lines.text: this guy thinks he can go back.
lines.review: An audience caption about an absent third person. It implies a trap but never supplies it.
